name: Case Topic and Definitions
description: Turn a resolution into a fair, debatable case.

lesson.title: Set a fair case topic
lesson.summary: Learn resolution, case topic, definitions, and contentions.

content.objective: Create a case topic with clear definitions and contentions.
content.explanation: A resolution is the broad prompt. A case topic is the specific debate you create from it. Definitions explain key terms, and contentions are the main reasons the case should win.
content.whyMatters: A fair case topic invites clash. If it is too vague, too narrow, or dependent on hidden knowledge, the round becomes less educational.

workedExample.prompt: Resolution: This House values education reform.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Case topic: public high schools should require a financial literacy course. Definitions: require means graduation requirement. Contentions: student debt prevention and practical career readiness.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer turns a broad resolution into a specific, debatable case.

choices: The specific issue debated from a resolution
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: The specific issue debated from a resolution
guidedQuestion.explanation: A case topic is the actual issue the round will debate.

practiceQuestions.explanation: Clear definitions help both sides understand what is being debated.

choices: A main reason for the case
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A main reason for the case
practiceQuestions.explanation: Contentions are the major arguments for the proposal.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What makes a fair case topic?
practiceQuestions.hint: Fair topics can be debated by both sides.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A fair case gives both sides a meaningful path to argue.

masteryCheck.prompt: A case topic is so narrow that opposition has no answer. What is the issue?
masteryCheck.explanation: A case should be specific but still debatable.

name: Claim, Warrant, Impact
description: Turn an idea into a complete argument the judge can evaluate.

lesson.title: Build a complete argument
lesson.summary: Learn the claim-warrant-impact pattern for stronger speeches.

content.objective: Write an argument with a clear claim, warrant, and impact.
content.explanation: A complete argument has three parts: the claim says what you believe, the warrant explains why it is true, and the impact explains why it matters in the round.
content.whyMatters: Judges cannot give full credit to an idea they cannot follow. This pattern makes your reasoning visible and gives later speeches something to extend.
steps: Name the claim in one direct sentence.
Add a warrant that explains the cause or logic.
End with the impact: who is affected, how much, and why it matters more than the other side.

workedExample.prompt: Schools should teach practical AI literacy.
workedExample.weakAnswer: AI literacy is important because AI is everywhere.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Schools should teach practical AI literacy because students already use AI tools for research and writing. If they learn limits, bias checks, and responsible use, they make fewer mistakes and are better prepared for college and work.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer states a claim, explains the mechanism, and gives a concrete impact.

choices: Schools should teach practical AI literacy.
Students already use AI tools for research and writing.
Prepared students make fewer mistakes in college and work.
This debate is about education policy.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Students already use AI tools for research and writing.
guidedQuestion.hint: The warrant is the reason the claim is true.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This sentence explains why AI literacy belongs in school: students are already using the tools.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which answer has all three parts?
choices: We affirm because the plan is good.
The plan improves safety because trained students can identify AI errors before relying on them, which reduces academic and workplace harm.
The negative side has no evidence.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The plan improves safety because trained students can identify AI errors before relying on them, which reduces academic and workplace harm.
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for claim, reason, and why it matters.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This choice includes the position, the mechanism, and the impact.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should come after a claim?
practiceQuestions.hint: The next step is explaining why the claim is true.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A warrant connects the claim to logic or evidence.

practiceQuestions.hint: Ask: why should the judge care?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The impact explains the importance or consequence of the argument.

masteryCheck.prompt: A judge asks why your argument matters. Which part are they asking for?
masteryCheck.hint: The word matters points to the consequence.
masteryCheck.explanation: Impact tells the judge why the argument should affect the decision.

name: Clash
description: Find the real disagreement and answer it directly.

lesson.title: Create direct clash
lesson.summary: Learn how to identify and resolve the main disagreement.

content.objective: Identify what both sides disagree about and answer that point directly.
content.explanation: Clash happens when two arguments meet on the same point. It starts with finding what the two sides actually disagree about — not what they both accept. A responsive answer targets the opponent's reasoning on that disputed point: repeating your own case is not clash, and answering a claim the opponent never made is not clash either. The strongest clash goes one step further and explains why your direct answer changes the disputed issue in your favour.
content.whyMatters: Rounds are won on comparison. Clash shows the judge that you are not just speaking well, you are winning the debate.
steps: Explain why your answer matters more or proves their claim wrong.

workedExample.prompt: Opponent says the plan costs too much.
workedExample.strongAnswer: On cost, they assume a new class is required. Our plan uses existing advisory time, so their budget objection does not apply.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer names the opposing argument and directly removes its assumption.

choices: On cost, their objection assumes a new class, but our plan uses advisory time.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: On cost, their objection assumes a new class, but our plan uses advisory time.
guidedQuestion.hint: Look for a direct answer to the other side.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This response meets the cost argument directly.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Side A argues a longer lunch break improves focus in afternoon classes. Side B argues the schedule cannot fit a longer lunch without cutting class time. Where is the real disagreement?
choices: Whether the schedule can absorb a longer lunch, since Side B never disputed the focus benefit
Whether focus matters in afternoon classes
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Whether the schedule can absorb a longer lunch, since Side B never disputed the focus benefit
practiceQuestions.hint: Find the point Side B actually contests.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Side B accepts the focus claim and attacks the schedule fit, so that is where the clash lives. Engaging anything else answers a point nobody disputed.

choices: They say cost, we answer with existing time.
They say safety, we answer with training.
Our first contention is still true.
They say delay, we answer with phase-in.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Our first contention is still true.
practiceQuestions.hint: Repeating your case is not direct clash.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This does not answer a specific opposing argument.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The opponent argues a school garden takes up field space used for sports. Which reply creates clash?
choices: Gardens teach responsibility, which is our first contention.
The garden plan uses the unused corner lot, so no field space is lost.
Sports are also valuable to students.
We will now summarise our own case.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The garden plan uses the unused corner lot, so no field space is lost.
practiceQuestions.hint: Which reply meets the space objection itself?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only the corner-lot answer engages the opponent's actual objection. Restating your contention or agreeing sports matter leaves the space argument standing.

masteryCheck.prompt: If the opponent says your plan is unrealistic, what should you answer first?

name: Constructive Speeches
description: Build the first version of your case clearly and strategically.

lesson.title: Build a constructive speech
lesson.summary: Learn what belongs in the first major speech.

content.objective: Write a constructive speech with definitions, contentions, and impacts.
content.explanation: A constructive speech builds the foundation of the round. It should define the topic, present major contentions, and explain impacts.
content.whyMatters: Later speeches depend on this foundation. If the constructive is vague, rebuttals become harder and the judge has less to evaluate.
steps: Explain the warrant and impact for each contention.

workedExample.prompt: Opening government speech on AI literacy.
workedExample.weakAnswer: AI literacy is good and students need it.
workedExample.strongAnswer: We define AI literacy as practical training in responsible tool use. Contention one: it improves academic integrity because students learn limits and citation habits. Contention two: it improves career readiness because students practice safe workplace use.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer defines terms and creates organized contentions.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What belongs in a constructive speech?
guidedQuestion.explanation: A constructive speech sets terms and introduces major arguments.

practiceQuestions.explanation: A contention is a main argument supporting the case.
Clear definitions prevent confusion and focus the round.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many contentions are usually easier for beginners?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Two or three contentions are manageable and distinct.

masteryCheck.prompt: If the judge cannot tell what your plan means, what did you likely miss?
masteryCheck.explanation: Definitions clarify the case and prevent confusion.

name: Evidence Evaluation
description: Judge whether evidence actually supports the claim being made.

lesson.title: Judge the evidence
lesson.summary: Decide how much a piece of evidence really proves, and compare competing evidence.

content.objective: Evaluate whether evidence genuinely supports an argument, and explain why one piece of evidence deserves more weight than another.
content.explanation: Evidence only helps an argument when it actually supports the specific claim being made. To judge a piece of evidence, ask four things. FIT: does it address this exact claim, or something merely nearby? SOURCE: who produced it, is their expertise relevant, and are there incentives that call for extra scrutiny? METHOD: how was the conclusion reached — who was studied, was there a real comparison, could something else explain the result? INTERPRETATION: does the conclusion claimed actually follow, or is the speaker stretching the evidence past what it shows? When two pieces of evidence conflict, compare them on these same questions instead of picking the one you like.
content.whyMatters: Rounds are full of confident citations. The debater who can say WHY one piece of evidence deserves more weight — not just that a source exists — gives the judge a reason to prefer their side, and spots the moment an opponent's conclusion goes further than their evidence.
steps: Check fit: restate the exact claim and ask whether the evidence is about that claim.
Check source and method: relevant expertise, reasons for caution, who was studied, and whether anything else could explain the result.
Check the conclusion: say plainly what the evidence does prove, and challenge whatever is claimed beyond that.

workedExample.prompt: Claim: removing library late fees gets more books returned on time. Two pieces of (hypothetical) evidence: A - a survey where members say they would return books on time without fees; B - return rates tracked at two similar libraries, where only the one that removed fees improved.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Evidence A is more recent, so it is better.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Evidence B deserves more weight. It measures actual returns rather than what people say they would do, and the unchanged library gives a comparison that points at the fee change itself. A is about intentions, which often differ from behaviour — it fits the topic, but B fits the claim.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer compares the two pieces on fit and method — measured behaviour with a comparison versus stated intentions — instead of using a shortcut like recency.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Claim: the new crosswalk made the street safer. Evidence: accidents fell in the month after it was installed. What is the biggest weakness?
choices: One month with no comparison cannot show the crosswalk caused the drop
The evidence is about the wrong street
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: One month with no comparison cannot show the crosswalk caused the drop
guidedQuestion.hint: Think about what else could explain one short window.
guidedQuestion.explanation: A short window with no comparison leaves the drop open to chance and season. The evidence is relevant, but it cannot yet carry the causal claim.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Claim: the gym renovation improved student fitness. Evidence: a survey shows students like the new gym. What is the problem?
choices: The evidence measures enjoyment, not fitness, so it does not fit the claim
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The evidence measures enjoyment, not fitness, so it does not fit the claim
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare what was measured with what is claimed.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Credible evidence can still fail to support the specific claim. Liking the gym is real information — about enjoyment, not fitness.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Neighbourhoods with more streetlights have less litter. A speaker concludes streetlights prevent litter. What should a careful debater say?
choices: Something else, like overall upkeep, could produce both — this needs a comparison before the causal claim stands
Streetlights are too expensive to matter
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Something else, like overall upkeep, could produce both — this needs a comparison before the causal claim stands
practiceQuestions.hint: Two things appearing together is not yet cause.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The association is real evidence, but well-kept neighbourhoods may get both lights and less litter. Without a comparison that separates the factors, the causal conclusion overreaches.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two reports on a teen curfew disagree. One, from a group campaigning for curfews, highlights a single town that improved. The other, an independent review of many towns with its method disclosed, found mixed results. Which deserves more weight and why?
choices: The independent review — it covers the whole pattern and shows its method, while the campaign report highlights one favourable case
The campaign report, because it is more confident
The campaign report, because one clear example beats many mixed ones
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The independent review — it covers the whole pattern and shows its method, while the campaign report highlights one favourable case
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare breadth, method and incentives — do not just pick a side.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Disagreement is where evaluation starts. An incentive to persuade plus a single selected example warrants caution; breadth and a disclosed method warrant more confidence. That is comparison, not source-bashing.

masteryCheck.prompt: Claim: a reading app doubled students' reading skill. Evidence: the app company surveyed volunteer users, who reported big improvement. What is the strongest evaluation?
choices: Self-selected users self-reporting, gathered by the seller, cannot support a claim as strong as 'doubled' — the conclusion outruns the evidence
The evidence is fine because the company knows its own app best
Reading skill cannot be measured, so the claim is meaningless
The study is acceptable because many users responded
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Self-selected users self-reporting, gathered by the seller, cannot support a claim as strong as 'doubled' — the conclusion outruns the evidence
masteryCheck.hint: Stack the problems: who gathered it, who answered, what was measured, what is claimed.
masteryCheck.explanation: Each issue alone calls for caution; together — seller incentive, volunteers, self-report, and a precise 'doubled' claim — the evidence cannot carry the conclusion. Naming that gap is exactly the skill.

name: Parliamentary Debate Roles
description: Understand what each side and speech is trying to do.

lesson.title: Know your parliamentary role
lesson.summary: Learn the jobs of government and opposition speakers.

content.objective: Match your speech choices to your role in parliamentary debate.
content.explanation: Government builds and defends a case. Opposition tests the case, offers counter-pressure, and explains why the proposal should not stand.
content.whyMatters: Knowing the role prevents scattered speeches and helps teams coordinate.
steps: Government defines and builds the case.
Opposition answers the case and creates clash.
Later speeches extend, refute, and weigh.

workedExample.prompt: Opposition hears a vague government case.
workedExample.weakAnswer: We have our own unrelated topic.
workedExample.strongAnswer: We challenge the definition because it is too broad, then argue the plan does not solve the stated problem.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer performs the opposition role by testing the case.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What is the government's first job?
guidedQuestion.explanation: Government must define and defend the case.

practiceQuestions.explanation: Opposition should explain why the government case fails or is not best.

practiceQuestions.hint: Roles tell each speaker what to do.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Role awareness keeps the team coordinated.
Government should clarify the terms of its case.

masteryCheck.prompt: If you are opposition, what should you do with a weak definition?
choices: Challenge how it shapes the debate
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Challenge how it shapes the debate
masteryCheck.explanation: Opposition can pressure definitions that make the debate unclear or unfair.

name: Rebuttal Speeches
description: Collapse to the arguments that decide the round.

lesson.title: Win the rebuttal
lesson.summary: Learn how rebuttals should answer, extend, and weigh.

content.objective: Use rebuttal time to resolve the round, not restart it.
content.explanation: A rebuttal speech should answer the most important opposing arguments, extend your best offense, and explain the voters.
content.whyMatters: Rebuttals are where judges often decide the round. A focused rebuttal is stronger than a rushed list.

workedExample.strongAnswer: This round comes down to feasibility versus preparedness. We win feasibility because the plan uses advisory time, and we win preparedness because the impact is immediate and long term.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer collapses to the central comparison.

guidedQuestion.explanation: Rebuttals should focus on the arguments most likely to decide the round.

practiceQuestions.explanation: Collapsing helps the judge see the decisive issues.

choices: A reason the judge should decide for you
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A reason the judge should decide for you
practiceQuestions.explanation: A voter tells the judge why your side should win.

practiceQuestions.hint: Late new material is usually unfair and confusing.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rebuttals should resolve existing arguments rather than introduce fresh case offense.

masteryCheck.prompt: A final speech introduces a brand-new contention. What is the problem?
choices: It is a new argument in rebuttal
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: It is a new argument in rebuttal
masteryCheck.explanation: Rebuttal speeches should not surprise opponents with new major arguments.

name: Refutation
description: Use a repeatable pattern to answer opposing arguments.

lesson.title: Answer with refutation
lesson.summary: Use they say, but, because, therefore to build strong rebuttal answers.

content.objective: Write a direct refutation using a clear four-part structure.
content.explanation: Refutation is the skill of answering the other side. A simple structure is: they say, but, because, therefore.
content.whyMatters: This keeps rebuttals from becoming scattered. It also makes your answer easy for the judge to evaluate.
steps: Therefore: tell the judge what to do with it.

workedExample.prompt: They say AI literacy wastes class time.
workedExample.strongAnswer: They say AI literacy wastes class time, but it can fit inside existing advisory lessons because schools already use that time for digital citizenship. Therefore, the time-cost argument is smaller than our preparedness benefit.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer identifies, answers, explains, and weighs the argument.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which part explains the reason the answer is true?
guidedQuestion.hint: The word because usually introduces the warrant.
guidedQuestion.explanation: The because part gives the reasoning behind the refutation.

choices: Tells the judge the result of the answer
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Tells the judge the result of the answer
practiceQuestions.explanation: Therefore explains how the judge should treat the argument after your answer.

choices: They say it costs too much, but the plan uses existing resources because advisory time already exists, so cost is not a voter.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: They say it costs too much, but the plan uses existing resources because advisory time already exists, so cost is not a voter.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This answer identifies the claim, answers it, explains why, and gives a result.
Vague denial does not explain why the opposing argument fails.

masteryCheck.prompt: In 'They say X, but Y because Z,' what is Y?
masteryCheck.explanation: Y is the direct answer to the opponent's claim.

name: Debate Round Orientation
description: Understand what happens in a debate round before your first practice.

lesson.title: How a debate round works
lesson.summary: What debate is, what each side is doing, and what the judge needs from you.

content.objective: Understand what a debate round is and what you are trying to do in one.
content.explanation: A debate round is a structured disagreement: two sides give reasons for different positions, answer each other, and a judge decides which side argued more persuasively. Your job is not just to speak — it is to help the judge see what your side claims, why it is true, why the other side's answers do not defeat it, and why your strongest points should decide the round. An argument is a claim backed by a reason and a why-it-matters; the Claim, Warrant, Impact lesson teaches how to build one. Early speaking in a round is mostly constructive — introducing and building your side's case. Later speaking is mostly responsive — answering what has already been argued and comparing the two sides. Formats differ in speech names, order and timing, but these jobs stay the same.
content.whyMatters: Beginners who enter a round without knowing the goal tend to list facts or repeat themselves. Judges can only vote on what they can follow: once you know the judge is deciding between reasons, every sentence gets a purpose — building a point, answering one, or explaining why yours matters more.
steps: Know your side's position and the strongest reasons for it.
Track what the other side actually argues, and answer it directly instead of repeating yourself.
Tell the judge which argument you are on and why your most important points should decide the round.

workedExample.prompt: A short exchange on whether the school day should start later.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Side A: Later starts are good. Side B: No, they are not. Side A: Yes, they really are.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Side A: A later start helps because students sleep more and focus better in class. Side B: But buses and family schedules make a later start hard for many households. Side A: Schedules can be adjusted once — lost focus in every class is a cost that repeats every single day.
workedExample.whyItWorks: Each side makes a claim with a reason, the reply answers that claim directly, and the final turn explains why one concern should matter more to the judge. That is a debate round in miniature.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What is a debater's real job in a round?
choices: Help the judge see why your side's reasons should win
Avoid mentioning the other side's points
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Help the judge see why your side's reasons should win
guidedQuestion.hint: Think about who decides the round.
guidedQuestion.explanation: The judge decides between reasons. Everything you say should help the judge understand your side's reasoning and prefer it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the goal of a debate round?
choices: Persuade the judge that your side's position is stronger
Prove the other team is dishonest
Say as many separate points as possible
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Persuade the judge that your side's position is stronger
practiceQuestions.hint: The judge is the audience that matters.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Every speech exists to persuade the judge — not to overwhelm, insult, or outlast the other side.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which choice gives the judge an actual reason instead of only stating a position?
choices: School uniforms help because they reduce visible income differences between students
Uniforms are a topic people discuss
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: School uniforms help because they reduce visible income differences between students
practiceQuestions.hint: An argument carries a reason the judge can weigh.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A claim plus a reason gives the judge something to evaluate. The other options assert or observe without giving a reason.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The other side just answered one of your arguments. What should you do?
choices: Respond to their answer and explain why your point still stands
Repeat your original sentence more confidently
Ignore it and move to a new topic
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Respond to their answer and explain why your point still stands
practiceQuestions.hint: An unanswered response usually wins the point.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Debate is exchange: once your argument is answered, the judge needs your response to the answer — not a louder restatement.

masteryCheck.prompt: Side A says: 'Homework should be limited because students need sleep.' Side B answers: 'Students lose sleep to phones, not homework.' What does the judge most need from Side A next?
choices: Why homework is still a real cause of lost sleep worth acting on, even if phones matter too
A louder restatement that sleep is important
A brand-new argument about grades instead
A comment about Side B's sincerity
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Why homework is still a real cause of lost sleep worth acting on, even if phones matter too
masteryCheck.hint: The clash is about the cause — resolve it.
masteryCheck.explanation: Side B answered the reason, so the judge needs Side A to engage that answer and explain why the original concern survives it. Responding to the response is the heart of debating.

name: Signposting
description: Make your speech easy to flow with clear labels and transitions.

lesson.title: Guide the judge through your speech
lesson.summary: Use labels, numbers, and transitions so the judge never gets lost.

content.objective: Use signposts to organize arguments out loud.
content.explanation: A signpost is a short label that tells listeners where you are in the speech. Good signposting sounds like: first, on their evidence, now on impact comparison.
content.whyMatters: Debate judges track arguments quickly. If they cannot place your response on the flow, even a smart answer may be missed.
steps: Label each argument before explaining it.
Use transition phrases when you move to a new issue.

workedExample.prompt: Respond to two arguments about cost and safety.
workedExample.weakAnswer: That is wrong because the cost is lower and safety is better too.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I have two answers. First, on cost: the plan uses existing advisory time, so the budget impact is small. Second, on safety: teaching responsible use reduces risky shortcuts.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer numbers the responses and names the issue before explaining.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which phrase is the clearest signpost?
guidedQuestion.hint: A signpost names where the judge should place the response.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This phrase tells the judge the speaker is moving to the cost argument.

choices: Tell the judge the order of the speech
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Tell the judge the order of the speech
practiceQuestions.explanation: A preview helps the judge follow the structure before details begin.

practiceQuestions.hint: The best transition names the next flow location.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This transition clearly identifies where the response belongs.

choices: It makes arguments easier to follow
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: It makes arguments easier to follow
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what helps a judge flow.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Judges reward arguments they can understand and place on the flow.

masteryCheck.prompt: You are answering the opponent's evidence. What should your signpost mention?
masteryCheck.hint: Name the argument area you are answering.
masteryCheck.explanation: A targeted signpost tells the judge this answer belongs on the evidence flow.

name: Weighing Arguments
description: Compare impacts so the judge knows which argument matters more.

lesson.title: Explain why your impact wins
lesson.summary: Use magnitude, probability, and timeframe to compare arguments.

content.objective: Compare impacts instead of only listing them.
content.explanation: Weighing explains why one argument matters more than another. Magnitude, probability, timeframe, and reversibility are useful names for common comparison moves — the skill is making the comparison clear, not saying the lens words.
content.whyMatters: Judges often believe both sides have some truth. Weighing tells them which truth should decide the round.
steps: Explain why your impact wins under that lens.

workedExample.prompt: Aff says preparedness; Neg says class time.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Preparedness outweighs class time on timeframe and reversibility. Lost class time is small and adjustable, but students using AI irresponsibly can create immediate academic and career consequences.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer compares both impacts and explains why one should decide the round — the lens names just make that comparison easy to follow.

choices: Our impact is bigger and happens sooner
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Our impact is bigger and happens sooner
guidedQuestion.explanation: This phrase compares magnitude and timeframe.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Aff wins a jobs impact; Neg wins a housing-cost impact. Which response weighs them?
choices: Jobs matter more here because lost income reaches more families and cannot be recovered quickly
Our jobs argument is very strong
The Neg is simply wrong about housing
We made more arguments than they did
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Jobs matter more here because lost income reaches more families and cannot be recovered quickly
practiceQuestions.hint: Weighing compares the two impacts against each other.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only this answer compares the two impacts and says why one should matter more. That comparison is weighing, whatever words it uses.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Their impact is huge but very unlikely; yours is smaller but nearly certain. Which comparison resolves that honestly?
choices: Prefer the near-certain impact, because a harm that will almost surely happen should beat one that probably never does
The huge impact automatically wins because it is bigger
Tell the judge to ignore likelihood
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Prefer the near-certain impact, because a harm that will almost surely happen should beat one that probably never does
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare how likely each impact is, not only its size.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This weighs likelihood against size and tells the judge why likelihood should decide here. A speaker can make this move without ever saying the word probability.

choices: To help the judge decide between impacts
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To help the judge decide between impacts
practiceQuestions.explanation: Weighing turns competing impacts into a clear decision.

masteryCheck.prompt: Your harm begins now; theirs arrives years away. Which sentence weighs that difference?
choices: Our harm is already starting, so the judge should act on it before their distant harm can even begin
Their impact is in the future, so it must be false
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Our harm is already starting, so the judge should act on it before their distant harm can even begin
masteryCheck.hint: Explain why sooner should matter to the decision.
masteryCheck.explanation: This uses the time difference to tell the judge why one impact should decide the round — timeframe weighing, whether or not the word is said.

name: Identifying the Problem
description: Separate symptoms from the real business issue.

lesson.title: Find the root business problem
lesson.summary: Choose a recommendation that solves the real issue.

content.objective: State the root problem before proposing a solution.
content.explanation: A symptom is what you notice. The root problem is why it is happening. Strong DECA answers solve the root problem.
content.whyMatters: Judges want business reasoning, not just activity. Identifying the real problem makes your solution more strategic.
steps: Choose the problem your solution can affect.

workedExample.prompt: A cafe has many first-time customers but few return.
workedExample.weakAnswer: The problem is not enough customers.
workedExample.strongAnswer: The problem is weak customer retention, not awareness. The solution should focus on loyalty and post-visit engagement.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer separates awareness from retention.

guidedQuestion.prompt: A cafe has many first visits but few repeat visits. What is the root problem?
guidedQuestion.hint: Repeat visits are about coming back.
guidedQuestion.explanation: The issue is retaining customers after the first visit.

choices: An observable sign of a deeper issue
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: An observable sign of a deeper issue
practiceQuestions.explanation: Symptoms help you infer the root problem.
A clear problem frames the recommendation.
A loyalty program directly targets repeat visits.

masteryCheck.prompt: If sales are down because checkout is slow, what should you target?
masteryCheck.explanation: Slow checkout points to operations, not only promotion.

name: Professional Communication
description: Present recommendations with executive clarity and confidence.

lesson.title: Sound like a business advisor
lesson.summary: Use concise structure, business vocabulary, and a confident close.

content.objective: Communicate with a clear opening, numbered points, and professional tone.
content.explanation: Professional communication is not fancy language. It means the judge can trust you because your answer is clear, calm, and business-focused.
content.whyMatters: DECA judges often score delivery and organization alongside the business idea.
steps: Open with the problem and goal.
Give two or three numbered recommendations.
Close with the expected result and how to measure it.

workedExample.weakAnswer: I would do social media and stuff.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I recommend a two-part promotion plan: first, targeted short-form videos for local students; second, a referral offer measured by new customer sign-ups.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer is organized, specific, and measurable.

choices: I have a two-part plan to improve repeat visits.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: I have a two-part plan to improve repeat visits.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This opening frames the goal and structure.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many recommendation points are usually manageable?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Two or three points allow enough depth without overload.
A measurable close shows business reasoning.
This phrase gives the judge a concrete metric.

masteryCheck.explanation: Executive clarity helps the judge understand and trust the recommendation.

name: Reading Scenarios
description: Quickly identify role, task, audience, and constraints in a DECA prompt.

lesson.title: Read a business scenario
lesson.summary: Find the job to be done before building your recommendation.

content.objective: Extract the role, problem, audience, and constraints from a scenario.
content.explanation: Before solving, pause and mark four things: who you are, who you are speaking to, what problem matters most, and what limits your solution.
content.whyMatters: DECA roleplays reward relevant solutions. If you miss the real scenario, even a polished presentation can score low.
steps: List constraints such as budget, time, staff, or brand.

workedExample.prompt: You are a marketing assistant speaking to a store owner about low repeat visits.
workedExample.strongAnswer: My role is marketing assistant, the audience is the owner, the problem is low repeat visits, and the solution must improve loyalty without assuming a huge budget.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer reads the situation before solving it.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which detail is the business problem?
guidedQuestion.hint: The problem is what needs to improve.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Low repeat visits is the challenge the recommendation must solve.

practiceQuestions.hint: Know who you are and who hears the answer.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Role and audience shape tone and recommendation.
Constraints help you recommend something the business can actually do.
Limited staff affects what solution is realistic.

masteryCheck.prompt: If the judge is a store owner, how should your tone sound?
masteryCheck.explanation: A business owner expects concise, useful recommendations.

name: Healthcare Ethics
description: Make responsible choices using safety, privacy, and respect.

lesson.title: Reason through healthcare ethics
lesson.summary: Use privacy, consent, safety, and fairness to evaluate scenarios.

content.objective: Use ethical principles to choose a safe and respectful response.
content.explanation: Healthcare ethics often involves balancing values like privacy, patient choice, safety, and professional responsibility.
content.whyMatters: HOSA scenarios may test what you do when the easy answer is not the most responsible answer.
steps: Explain why it respects the patient.

workedExample.prompt: A friend asks about a patient's condition.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Tell them if they promise not to share.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I cannot share private patient information. I would direct them to the proper contact process and protect confidentiality.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer protects privacy and gives a professional next step.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which principle is involved when protecting patient information?
guidedQuestion.explanation: Patient information should be protected unless sharing is authorized.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should you do with private patient information?
choices: Share only through appropriate authorized channels
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Share only through appropriate authorized channels
practiceQuestions.explanation: Professional ethics requires protecting patient information.
Respecting dignity supports professional care.

practiceQuestions.hint: Judges need to see your decision process.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Explaining the principle makes the answer stronger.

masteryCheck.prompt: A scenario involves risk of harm. What principle becomes urgent?
masteryCheck.explanation: Safety is central when someone could be harmed.

name: Medical Terminology Basics
description: Break clinical words into roots, prefixes, and suffixes.

lesson.title: Decode medical terms
lesson.summary: Use word parts to understand unfamiliar health terms.

content.objective: Break medical terms into word parts and explain them accurately.
content.explanation: Many medical terms are built from prefixes, roots, and suffixes. If you can identify parts, you can understand unfamiliar terms more safely.
content.whyMatters: HOSA events reward accurate health science language. Terminology also helps you communicate clearly with patients and judges.
steps: Put the meaning together and check context.

workedExample.strongAnswer: Tachy means fast and cardia relates to the heart, so tachycardia means a fast heart rate.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer uses word parts and avoids vague guessing.

guidedQuestion.prompt: In tachycardia, what does tachy mean?

practiceQuestions.explanation: Cardi/cardio refers to the heart.

practiceQuestions.hint: Word parts are clues, not the whole clinical picture.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Word parts help decode terms while still respecting context.
This answer is accurate and appropriately limited.

masteryCheck.explanation: Hypo often means low, under, or deficient.

name: Patient Communication
description: Explain health information clearly, respectfully, and safely.

lesson.title: Communicate with patients clearly
lesson.summary: Use empathy, plain language, and confirmation checks.

content.objective: Explain health information in plain language and confirm understanding.
content.explanation: Patient communication combines accuracy and empathy. A strong response avoids jargon, listens to concerns, and checks understanding.
content.whyMatters: In healthcare, communication affects safety. Patients need to understand next steps, risks, and when to ask for help.

workedExample.prompt: A patient is nervous about a blood pressure reading.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Your systolic is elevated; just calm down.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I understand this number can feel stressful. Blood pressure can change for many reasons, so we will recheck it and share it with the provider. Can you tell me what step we are taking next?
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer is empathetic, clear, and checks understanding.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which response best uses plain language?
choices: We will recheck your blood pressure and talk with the provider.
Your systolic parameter requires clinical correlation.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: We will recheck your blood pressure and talk with the provider.
guidedQuestion.hint: Plain language is accurate and understandable.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This response avoids jargon and gives a safe next step.

choices: Asking the patient to explain the next step in their own words
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Asking the patient to explain the next step in their own words
practiceQuestions.explanation: Teach-back helps confirm the patient understands.
A calm tone supports professionalism and patient safety.
Plain language improves comprehension without sacrificing accuracy.

masteryCheck.prompt: A patient says they are confused. What should you do?
choices: Pause and explain again in simpler language
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Pause and explain again in simpler language
masteryCheck.explanation: Clear communication includes adapting when the patient is confused.

name: Evidence-Based Reasoning
description: Support claims with examples, reasoning, and responsible evidence.

lesson.title: Support your message with evidence
lesson.summary: Make speeches more credible with support and explanation.

content.objective: Use evidence and reasoning to support a public speaking claim.
content.explanation: Evidence can be an example, data point, expert idea, or personal story. Reasoning explains how the evidence proves the claim.
content.whyMatters: Audiences are more likely to trust a message when they can see why it is true.
steps: Tie it back to the audience.

workedExample.strongAnswer: Practice improves confidence because repeated rehearsal makes the speech feel familiar. For example, a student who practices the opening five times is less likely to freeze when starting.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer gives reasoning and a concrete example.

choices: Explains how evidence proves the claim
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Explains how evidence proves the claim
guidedQuestion.explanation: Reasoning connects support to the claim.

practiceQuestions.explanation: Examples can function as evidence when they prove a point.

choices: So the audience understands its meaning
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: So the audience understands its meaning
practiceQuestions.hint: Do not make listeners infer everything.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Explanation turns evidence into persuasion.

choices: Practice helps because familiarity reduces fear at the start.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Practice helps because familiarity reduces fear at the start.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This answer gives a reason that supports the claim.

masteryCheck.prompt: A story supports your point only if you also do what?
masteryCheck.explanation: The speaker must show how the story proves the message.

name: Presentation Structure
description: Organize speeches with a clear opening, body, and close.

lesson.title: Structure a clear speech
lesson.summary: Build a speech listeners can follow from start to finish.

content.objective: Use a simple structure: hook, thesis, main points, and close.
content.explanation: Strong speeches feel easy to follow because each part has a job. The opening earns attention, the thesis states the message, the body proves it, and the close makes it memorable.
content.whyMatters: Structure lowers anxiety and helps audiences remember your message.
steps: Organize two or three main points.
Close by returning to the main message.

workedExample.prompt: Speech about why students should learn public speaking.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Public speaking is good and helps people.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Have you ever had a great idea but felt too nervous to say it? Public speaking helps students turn ideas into action. I will show how it builds confidence, clarity, and leadership.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer has a hook, thesis, and preview.

guidedQuestion.hint: The thesis tells the audience what the speech argues.
guidedQuestion.explanation: A thesis gives the speech direction.

practiceQuestions.explanation: The opening should earn attention and state the message.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why use two or three main points?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A small number of main points improves clarity.

practiceQuestions.hint: The close should land the speech.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong close reinforces the central idea.

masteryCheck.prompt: If an audience cannot tell your main point, what is likely missing?
masteryCheck.hint: The thesis is the main message.
masteryCheck.explanation: A clear thesis helps the audience understand the speech's purpose.
